1.title: Welcome & Erasmus+ Context
1.text: Welcome to Istituto Lagrange in Milan! We are delighted to host visiting European colleagues through Erasmus Plus. Here in Northern Italy, technical education has deep historical roots. In this presentation, we take you inside our fourth-year telecommunications classroom, class 4B INF, where physics, history, and hands-on laboratory discovery come together. Every module in this deck includes an interactive simulator, so feel free to experiment as we go!

2.title: The Italian Technical High School System
2.text: Italy's Istituto Tecnico Tecnologico offers a distinctive five-year journey. Following a two-year scientific and cultural foundation, students enter the three-year triennio to specialize in Computer Science and Telecommunications. By age nineteen, our students do not just memorize theory; through over one hundred and fifty hours of industry internships, they graduate as certified technical specialists, ready for the European high-tech workforce or university engineering degrees.

3.title: Class 4B INF Syllabus Structure
3.text: Our fourth-year curriculum bridges classical physics with contemporary communication networks across five thematic pillars: signal geometry, Fourier analysis, optical guided media, analog and digital modulation, and network protocols. Nearly half of our class time is spent in the laboratory, where students verify physical principles with oscilloscopes and circuit prototypes rather than just taking formulas on faith.

4.title: Module 1: Signal Classification & Interactive Generator
4.text: Did you know that signal analysis began in a cathedral? In 1581, a young Galileo Galilei timed a swinging chandelier in Pisa using his own heartbeat, discovering that harmonic oscillations maintain a constant period regardless of their swing size! In telecommunications, we represent this with a simple cosine wave. Peak voltage is how far the wave swings, while RMS voltage measures the real muscle of the wave—the equivalent DC battery power that would heat a resistor. Play with the virtual oscilloscope below to see Galileo's harmonic motion in action!

5.title: Module 2: Fourier Analysis & Live Interactive Synth
5.text: In 1807, Jean-Baptiste Fourier presented a radical idea to the French Academy of Sciences: any repeating wave, no matter how jagged, can be built purely by adding together gentle sinusoidal flutes! The great mathematicians of his time, including Laplace and our school's namesake Joseph-Louis Lagrange, were openly skeptical! Fourier was originally trying to understand heat diffusion in Napoleon's artillery cannons, but his mathematical insight became the bedrock of modern telecommunications. In the simulator below, dial in harmonics to watch a jagged square wave emerge from pure sine waves!

6.title: Module 3: Fiber Optics & Total Internal Reflection
6.text: Today, fiber optic cables carry over ninety-five percent of global internet traffic. But the principle behind it was first demonstrated in 1854 as a Victorian parlor trick! The Irish physicist John Tyndall illuminated a stream of water pouring from a bucket, showing that light remained trapped inside the curving water jet. Just like a flat pebble skipping across a calm lake, light bounces off the boundary between the glass core and cladding without leaking, provided the launch angle stays above the critical angle. Test the skipping stone principle live in the optical simulator below!

7.title: Module 4: Modulation Systems & Signal Transmission
7.text: Imagine trying to transmit human speech across the continent using sound waves directly. At one kilohertz, an antenna would have to be seventy-five kilometers tall—higher than Mount Everest! Guglielmo Marconi and the radio pioneers solved this by inventing modulation. The human voice rides on top of a high-frequency carrier wave, like a passenger boarding an airplane. Whether we modulate the wave's height in AM, its rhythm in FM, or switch digital pulses in ASK and FSK, the carrier does the flying while our message arrives crystal clear. Try switching modulation modes below!

8.title: Module 5: DSO Bandwidth & Rule of 5
8.text: When Karl Ferdinand Braun invented the cathode ray oscilloscope in 1897, signals were slow and analog. But in today's high-speed digital electronics, clock pulses jump between zero and five volts in mere nanoseconds. In the lab, students learn the Rule of Five: your oscilloscope's bandwidth must be at least five times faster than the clock frequency. If your scope is too slow, it acts like a blurry camera shutter, cutting off the high Fourier harmonics and turning sharp square clock pulses into sluggish rounded waves. Watch how bandwidth limits our view in the scope simulator below!

9.title: Pedagogical Methodology & Link Budget Calculator
9.text: Why do telecom engineers speak in decibels instead of watts? In the 1920s, telephone engineers named the decibel after Alexander Graham Bell to match the natural logarithmic response of the human ear. A quiet whisper and a thunderclap differ in power by one hundred million times! Decibels transform difficult decimal multiplications into simple additions and subtractions. In our lab, students calculate the link budget: transmitter power in dBm, minus fiber cable loss, equals receiver power. Try the link budget calculator below to test single-mode versus multi-mode reach!

10.title: Our Digital Teaching Platform: fmorea.github.io
10.text: To keep learning accessible, serverless, and private, we built our open-source platform on GitHub Pages. It features offline neural speech narration powered by Kokoro ONNX models, instant exam revision with high-density compressed QR codes, and authenticated student certificates generated client-side with jsPDF. Everything is designed with zero server overhead and full compliance with European privacy standards and the EU AI Act.

11.title: Erasmus+ Bilateral Cooperation
11.text: We believe technical education thrives on international dialogue. Through Erasmus Plus Key Action 1 and 2, we warmly invite your school to collaborate with IIS Luigi Lagrange. Whether through teacher job shadowing, bilingual CLIL co-teaching, reciprocal vocational student internships in Milan's IT sector, or shared open educational resources, we can build enduring bilateral partnerships across Europe.

12.title: Conclusion & Contact Details
12.text: Thank you so much for exploring our telecommunications curriculum and digital platform! You can scan the QR code to keep the interactive deck on your smartphone, or contact Professor Fernando Morea to explore Erasmus Plus cooperation. As the European motto reminds us: enriching lives, opening minds through education. We look forward to welcoming you to Milan!
